case_name: Mustafa Tunç and Fecire Tunç v. Turkey
court: European Court of Human Rights, Grand Chamber

facts.text: Mustafa Tunç was born in 1946 and died in 2006. Fecire and Yüksel Tunç, born in 1952 and 1975 respectively, live in Istanbul. They are the father, mother and brother of Cihan Tunç, who was born on 20 November 1983 and died on 13 February 2004.

anchor.surface_text: 11.  Mustafa Tunç was born in 1946 and died in 2006. Fecire and Yüksel Tunç, born in 1952 and 1975 respectively, live in Istanbul. They are the father, mother and brother of Cihan Tunç, who was born on 20 November 1983 and died on 13 February 2004.

facts.text: Cihan Tunç joined the army in August 2003 to perform his compulsory military service. The medical report drawn up prior to his conscription stated that there were no contraindications to his conscription. He was not known to suffer from any psychological disorder or any other specific problem.

anchor.surface_text: 12.  Cihan Tunç joined the army in August 2003 to perform his compulsory military service. The medical report drawn up prior to his conscription stated that there were no contraindications to his conscription. He was not known to suffer from any psychological disorder or any other specific problem.

facts.text: On an unspecified date Cihan Tunç obtained the rank of corporal. Following a training exercise which ended on 31 November 2003, he qualified as a sergeant.

anchor.surface_text: 13.  On an unspecified date Cihan Tunç obtained the rank of corporal. Following a training exercise which ended on 31 November 2003, he qualified as a sergeant.

facts.text: He was then assigned to the protection of a site belonging to the private oil company NV Turkse Perenco (“Perenco”), for which the Kocaköy central gendarmerie was providing security services.

anchor.surface_text: 14.  He was then assigned to the protection of a site belonging to the private oil company NV Turkse Perenco (“Perenco”), for which the Kocaköy central gendarmerie was providing security services.

facts.text: On 13 February 2004, at about 5.50 a.m., Cihan Tunç was injured by gunfire at the guard post known as “tower no. 2”. He was one of the gendarmes on sentry duty and assigned to the guard post known as “tower no. 3”.

anchor.surface_text: 15.  On 13 February 2004, at about 5.50 a.m., he was injured by gunfire. He was one of the gendarmes on sentry duty and assigned to the guard post known as “tower no. 3”. The incident occurred at the guard post known as “tower no. 2”.

facts.text: Cihan Tunç was transported to hospital immediately after the incident by sergeant A.A. and private M.D., accompanied by private M.S., who was the last person to have seen Cihan Tunç before the incident.

anchor.surface_text: 16.  Cihan Tunç was transported to hospital immediately after the incident by sergeant A.A. and private M.D., accompanied by private M.S., who was the last person to have seen Cihan Tunç before the incident.

facts.text: Cihan Tunç was pronounced dead shortly after arrival at Diyarbakır Military Hospital.

anchor.surface_text: 17.  Cihan Tunç was pronounced dead shortly after arrival at Diyarbakır Military Hospital.

facts.text: The military prosecutor’s office of the 7th Army Corps, located in Diyarbakır, was informed immediately after the incident and a judicial investigation was opened as a matter of course.

anchor.surface_text: 18.  The military prosecutor’s office of the 7th Army Corps, located in Diyarbakır, was informed immediately after the incident and a judicial investigation was opened as a matter of course.

facts.text: A few hours after the incident, military prosecutor E.Ö. went to the hospital and was joined by a team of criminal investigation experts from the national gendarmerie. He also sent another team to the scene and asked the Kocaköy civilian prosecutor to attend to supervise initial investigations and secure evidence.

anchor.surface_text: 19.  A few hours after the incident, a member of that office, military prosecutor E.Ö., went to the hospital to which Cihan Tunç had been admitted and was joined there, on his instructions, by a team of criminal investigation experts from the national gendarmerie. In addition, he sent another team to the scene of the incident and asked the Kocaköy (civilian) prosecutor to attend, in order to supervise the initial investigations and take any measures necessary to secure evidence.

facts.text: On arrival at the hospital, the military prosecutor ordered an external examination of the corpse and an autopsy under his supervision. Several photos were taken, clothing removed and sent for analysis to determine shooting distance. Fingerprints and swabs were taken from the deceased and M.S., the last person to see Cihan alive, to check for gunpowder traces. The deceased’s pockets were emptied and inventoried.

anchor.surface_text: 20-21.  On his arrival at the hospital, the military prosecutor ordered that an external examination of the corpse and an autopsy be carried out, under his supervision. Several photos were taken of the corpse. The deceased’s clothing was removed and sent for laboratory analysis with a view to determining the distance from which the shot had been fired. Fingerprints were taken from the deceased and from M.S., who was the last person to have seen Cihan Tunç alive and could therefore have been involved in the incident. Swabs were also taken from their hands, to be checked for traces of gunpowder. Lastly, the deceased’s pockets were emptied and an inventory made of their contents.

facts.text: Forensic doctor L.E. examined the body and found the entry wound on the right side of the neck and exit wound on the left side of the back under the shoulder blade. No signs of blows or violence. Death caused by haemorrhage from bullet wound striking trachea and left lung. Shot probably fired at point-blank range based on residue material.

anchor.surface_text: 22-23.  The prosecutor then instructed forensic doctor L.E. to examine the body with a view to ascertaining the cause of death, and to make any observations he may have on the circumstances of the death. The forensic doctor recorded the following findings: body height, 1.75 metres; the entry wound, with an abrasion ring, was on the right side of the neck, and the exit wound, measuring 4 x 2 centimetres, was on the left side of the back, under the lower edge of the shoulder blade. The forensic doctor noted no trace on the body of blows or violence. He stated that death had occurred following a haemorrhage caused by a bullet wound, and that the bullet had struck the trachea and left lung. He also mentioned that the shot had probably been fired at point-blank range (yakın atış). He based that conclusion on the presence of certain residue material.

facts.text: Two unspent cartridges and a spent cartridge were found lying on the ground inside the sentry post. The ceiling had an impact mark resembling a shot. Small pieces of cement debris and large bloodstains were on the floor. The deceased’s weapon, a G-3 rifle, had been used recently; M.S.'s MG-3 rifle seemed unused. Both weapons sent for scientific analysis.

anchor.surface_text: 28-29.  The report further noted that two unspent cartridges and a spent cartridge were found lying on the ground inside the sentry post. The ceiling had an impact mark which resembled that of a shot. Small pieces of cement debris from the ceiling were found on the floor, which was also spattered with large bloodstains. The report also stated that a cursory examination of the deceased’s weapon, a G-3-type rifle which had been placed under lock and key pending the prosecutor’s arrival, indicated that it had been used a short time previously. According to the report, this weapon, as well as that assigned to private M.S., an MG-3-type rifle which seemed not to have been used, had been sent to a laboratory for scientific analysis.

facts.text: On 16 February 2004, the gendarmerie’s criminal research laboratory reported that lead, barium and antimony were found on the deceased’s hands, and barium and antimony on M.S.'s hands, residues from discharging a weapon. Gunpowder residues can transfer easily, especially during first aid. Tests on Cihan’s clothes indicated a shot fired at point-blank range.

anchor.surface_text: 33-34.  On 16 February 2004 the gendarmerie’s criminal research laboratory issued an expert report (report no. 2004/90/chemical). That report indicated that analysis of the samples taken from the deceased’s hands and from M.S., using the so-called “atomic absorption spectrometry” technique, had revealed the presence of lead, barium and antimony on the deceased’s hands, and of barium and antimony on those of M.S. After noting that those elements were residues from the discharging of a weapon, the report pointed out that gunpowder residues contained micrometric particles which passed very easily from one surface to another and that those residues frequently migrated to the hands when first aid was administered. The report also noted that the tests on Cihan Tunç’s clothes indicated that he had been the victim of a shot fired at point-blank range.

facts.text: On 17 February 2004, the Diyarbakır national police criminal laboratory confirmed that the spent cartridge came from Cihan Tunç’s weapon and that both rifles were operating normally.

anchor.surface_text: 35.  On 17 February 2004 the Diyarbakır national police criminal laboratory also issued its expert report (report no. BLS-2004/464), following ballistic tests carried out on the spent cartridge and on the two weapons found at the scene of the incident. The tests indicated that the two rifles were operating normally and confirmed that the spent cartridge came from Cihan Tunç’s weapon.

facts.text: M.S., the last person to see Cihan alive, stated that Cihan arrived 15-20 minutes before relieving him, was feeling down, played with his rifle, and then a shot was heard. M.S. denied shooting Cihan or having a dispute with him.

anchor.surface_text: 37-38.  In his evidence to the military prosecutor, M.S. stated: “Cihan arrived at the tower where I was on duty fifteen to twenty minutes before he was due to relive me... He told me that he was feeling down... He began playing with the cocking lever on his rifle... I was five or six metres from the tower when I heard a shot... I ran inside. [Cihan] was lying on the ground... I removed the rifle and tried to revive [Cihan]... Sergeant A.A. arrived...”. He confirmed he had no dispute with Cihan and had not shot him.

facts.text: Sergeant A.A. heard a gunshot, rushed to the spot with privates, found Cihan lying on the ground, attempted to find his pulse, and ordered transport to canteen then hospital. He stated only three guard posts were in use, with the incident at “low tower” aka “tower no. 2”.

anchor.surface_text: 46-47.  In his statement to the military prosecutor, sergeant A.A. indicated that he had heard a gunshot and, together with several privates, had rushed to the spot from where the sound had come. They found Cihan Tunç lying on the ground. After attempting to find the injured man’s pulse, A.A. ordered that he be transported to the canteen and then to hospital. He indicated that only three guard posts were in use... The second post, known as the “low tower”, although in reality located in fourth position from the entrance, was also known as “tower no. 2”.

facts.text: The administrative inquiry concluded the incident was an accident, considering absence of family, social or psychological problems, the position and distance of the shot, though the possibility of unlawful killing was considered initially.

anchor.surface_text: 58.  Having regard to the absence of family, social or psychological problems on the part of the deceased, the fact that he had been at a guard post assigned to one of his fellow servicemen and to the position and distance (point-blank range) of the shot, the inquiry concluded that the incident had been an accident. It seems, however, that the possibility of unlawful killing was considered at the beginning of the inquiry.

facts.text: On 30 June 2004, the prosecution service issued a decision not to bring a prosecution, finding no grounds to hold another person responsible for Cihan Tunç’s death, concluding the shot was fired accidentally while he was leaning to his right side with the rifle barrel pointed towards his neck.

anchor.surface_text: 59.  On 30 June 2004, holding that there were no grounds for finding that another person had been responsible for Cihan Tunç’s death, the prosecution service issued a decision not to bring a prosecution. The prosecutor set out all of the evidence gathered during the investigation. He concluded that the shot had been fired when the young man, with his chest bent, had been leaning towards his right side and the barrel of the rifle was pointed towards his neck...

facts.text: The applicants appealed the decision not to prosecute, alleging grey areas remained about the circumstances of Cihan Tunç’s death, particularly the bullet trajectory. They did not mention that M.D. had not been questioned or that no fingerprint tests had been conducted on the weapon.

anchor.surface_text: 62.  The applicants appealed against the decision, alleging that several grey areas remained as to the circumstances of Cihan Tunç’s death. In particular, they claimed that the trajectory followed by the bullet had not been clearly defined. They did not refer to the fact that M.D. had not been questioned, or that no fingerprint tests had been conducted on the weapon.

facts.text: On 14 October 2004, the military court of the Diyarbakır 2nd Air-force Corps upheld the applicants’ appeal and ordered additional investigation to clarify bullet trajectory and firing position, noting no plausible grounds for suicide and questioning gunpowder residue on M.S.'s hands.

anchor.surface_text: 63.  On 14 October 2004 the military court of the Diyarbakır 2nd Air-force Corps upheld the applicants’ appeal and ordered the prosecution service to carry out an additional investigation. In particular, it considered that the bullet’s trajectory and the firing position needed to be clearly established... It also indicated that no plausible grounds for suicide had been identified... It stated that no explanation had been provided for the gunshot residue on the hands of M.S., the last person to have seen Cihan Tunç before the incident.

facts.text: On 24 November 2004, the military prosecutor visited the Perenco site with three criminal investigation experts, carried out a reconstruction of events using a person similar in build to the deceased, and took steps to determine the bullet’s trajectory including using a string between the ceiling impact mark and rifle barrel.

anchor.surface_text: 64-66.  On 24 November 2004 the military prosecutor visited the Perenco site, accompanied by three criminal investigation experts... a reconstruction of the events was carried out, assisted by an individual who was similar in build to the deceased. Steps to determine the bullet’s trajectory were taken, including the use of a string, stretched between the impact mark on the ceiling and the barrel of a G-3 rifle.

facts.text: The experts concluded that Cihan Tunç had been sitting or crouching holding his rifle in his right hand; while attempting to stand up by leaning on his weapon with knees bent, his hand pulled the trigger and the shot was fired.

anchor.surface_text: 68.  In the light of all the evidence gathered, the experts reached the following conclusion: Cihan Tunç had been sitting or crouching and was holding his rifle in his right hand; while he was attempting to stand up by leaning on his weapon, and with his knees still bent, his hand had pulled the trigger and the shot had been fired.

facts.text: On 8 December 2004, the prosecutor completed investigations and sent the file to the military court with a report responding to the court’s requests, explaining gunshot residue on M.S.'s hands could have transferred during first aid, and that the firing position did not indicate suicide.

anchor.surface_text: 71-72.  On 8 December 2004 the prosecutor completed the investigations and sent the file to the military court... With regard to the traces of gunshot on the hands, he pointed out that the file contained an expert report indicating that gunshot residue was very volatile and that it could have moved from the dead man’s clothes or hands to M.S.’s hands immediately after the incident... As to determination of the bullet’s trajectory... the prosecutor stated... the hypothesis of suicide had not been entertained.

facts.text: On 17 December 2004, the military court dismissed the applicants’ appeal against the decision not to prosecute.

anchor.surface_text: 75.  On 17 December 2004 the military court dismissed the applicants’ appeal.

facts.text: The applicants submitted a private medical report by British expert Dr Allen M. Anscombe dated 11 October 2005, who reviewed case documents and concluded the autopsy findings were reasonable but brief, the bullet trajectory suggested the deceased was bent over when shot, and no signs of struggle were found.

anchor.surface_text: 77.  The applicants submitted a private medical report, prepared at their request by a British expert, Dr Allen M. Anscombe, and dated 11 October 2005... The expert... concluded... The autopsy report indicated... The photographs demonstrate... no possibility that entry and exit have been got “the wrong way round”... no autopsy signs that the deceased had been involved in a struggle or a fight.

facts.text: On 10 January 2007, the Supreme Military Administrative Court allowed the applicants’ claims in part, finding the death caused by careless handling of the service rifle, implying lack of sufficient training and negligence in supervision, awarding pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages to the family.

anchor.surface_text: 81.  On 10 January 2007 the court allowed the applicants’ claims in part. It noted that the death had been caused by careless handling of the service rifle. It considered that this implied a lack of sufficient training in handling weapons and negligence in the supervision and protection of conscripts... the Supreme Military Administrative Court awarded the following sums...

facts.text: On 21 April 2004, the Mehmetçik Foundation awarded financial assistance of over 3,000 euros to the deceased man’s family.

anchor.surface_text: 84.  On 21 April 2004 the Mehmetçik Foundation... awarded 4,916,700,000 former Turkish lira (a little over 3,000 euros at that date) to the deceased man’s family in financial assistance.
